When I say “RAG,” I mean the system first searches a knowledge base, then writes an answer using those sources.
The key point is: the model answers using verified context.
That reduces errors compared to a model that guesses from memory.
We run hybrid retrieval with BM25, ANN search, and cosine similarity, then feed results into a prompt template with chain-of-thought style reasoning and temperature control.
We also use LoRA fine-tuning on a transformer backbone, plus RLHF, to improve response quality across domains.
Today I’m pitching a platform that uses LLMs with RAG, vector embeddings, and a reranker to reduce hallucinations.
Our stack uses Kubernetes, Docker, Redis, and Postgres, and we deploy via CI/CD pipelines with observability through OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, and Grafana.
We built a tool that helps people get accurate answers from their own documents.
It works like this: first it searches for the most relevant parts of your files, then it writes an answer using only what it found.
This is useful because it reduces guessing and helps the user trust the result.
If the answer can’t be supported by the documents, the tool tells you it doesn’t have enough information instead of making something up.

Your body is like a big team of tiny workers, and each worker is called a cell.
When you get a cut, lots of these little workers rush over to the spot to fix it up.
Some cells are like construction workers — they patch the hole.
Others are like security guards — they fight off any germs that try to sneak in.
That's why most cuts heal on their own in a few days.
Your body knows what to do without you even thinking about it.
It's working on stuff like that all the time, even while you're asleep.
